back-field: the group of players behind the football line who run and kick
gridiron: the football field, or football itself, as a sport
basket-ball: an indoor game in which players score by throwing a ball through a hoop
diamond: the baseball field, with its bases arranged in a square
squad: a group of players chosen to train for a school team
candidates: people trying out for a place on a team or in a club
guard: a football player who blocks in the line beside the centre
corker: something outstandingly good, an excellent thing or person (slang)
chaps: fellows or young men; a casual, old-fashioned word for boys
chums: close friends who spend much of their time together
chummy: friendly and sociable, as close friends are with one another
bounder: an ill-mannered, dishonourable person who behaves badly toward others
rough-necks: rowdy, rough-mannered young men or troublemakers
tiddly-widdly: a nonsense expression, used to mock or dismiss something silly
suit-case: an old term for a small rectangular travelling bag
expressman: a deliveryman who carries parcels and goods for a delivery company
escritoire: an old-fashioned writing desk with drawers and a sloping lid
bureau: a chest of drawers for clothes, often with a mirror on top
chamber: an old word for a bedroom or private room
sitting-room: a room in a house used for relaxing and receiving visitors
spectacles: an old word for eyeglasses worn to correct or aid sight
countenance: a person's face or facial expression, showing their mood
bearing: a person's manner, posture, or way of carrying themselves
awfully: extremely or very, used as an intensifier in older speech
mighty: very or extremely, an informal and old-fashioned intensifier
presently: shortly or soon afterward, in an older sense of the word
forth: onward or out into view, an old-fashioned directional word
haltingly: in a hesitant, broken way, pausing as if unsure of the words
perplexedly: in a confused, puzzled way, unable to understand something
wistful: sadly longing for something one wants or has lost
ponderous: heavy, slow, and clumsy, as if weighed down by its own bulk
hospitable: welcoming and generous toward guests and strangers
obligingly: willingly and helpfully, doing someone a favour without fuss
apologetic: showing regret or sorrow for having caused some inconvenience
chuckled: laughed quietly and inwardly to oneself
proclaimed: announced publicly and formally, declaring something loudly
trifle: something very small or unimportant, or a small amount of something
scant: barely enough, very little in quantity or amount
expanses: wide, open stretches of land, water, or sky
relic: an old object surviving from the past, valued for its age
antique: old and valuable, made in an earlier period and admired for it
recitations: classroom sessions where pupils recite lessons aloud from memory
coupons: printed tickets or vouchers that can be exchanged for goods or services
lifework: the main task or purpose to which a person devotes their life
gymnasium: a large indoor hall fitted with equipment for physical exercise
tanned: having skin darkened by long exposure to the sun
ice-cream: a frozen sweet dessert made from cream and sugar
stuff: nonsense or foolish talk, or a general word for things
fixed: arranged or settled in a particular way, decided beforehand
dormitory: a large bedroom shared by several students in a school
snails: slow-moving people or things, used here as a joke or insult
to-morrow: the day after today, an older spelling of tomorrow
to-day: this present day, an older spelling of today
to-night: this coming evening or night, an older spelling of tonight
gulped: swallowed hard, often from nervousness, surprise, or emotion
half-way: midway between two points, at the midpoint of a distance
gravely: in a serious, solemn, or sombre manner
bath-robe: a loose garment worn over the body after bathing
frowned: drew the brows together in displeasure, worry, or thought
neared: came close to a place or thing in distance or time
